title: Single-atom detection with a quantum-controlled mechanical oscillator
authors: Maxime Perdriat, Maciej Dziewiecki, Josef-Anton Agner, Massimiliano Rossi, Frederic Merkt, Martin Frimmer, Lukas Novotny
abstract: Using supersonic expansion, we create a time-gated, directional beam of Xe atoms with a narrow momentum distribution and detect their collisions with a levitated nanosphere cooled to its quantum ground state. We observe individual momentum kicks below 50 keV/c with 96% confidence and distinguish directional momentum transfer from the atomic beam against the background of thermal collisions. Our experiments constitute a first step toward the exploration of distance-dependent short-range interactions between atoms and levitated systems, as well as toward the use of levitated platforms for impulsive force sensing in previously unexplored parameter regimes.
summary: This experiment demonstrates the detection of individual momentum kicks from colliding Xe atoms with a quantum-cooled, levitated nanosphere. By using matched filtering on the nanosphere's motion, the researchers confirmed the ability to measure impulsive forces with high precision. This advances the use of levitated systems as quantum sensors for studying fundamental atomic interactions.
main_problem: The research aims to explore distance-dependent short-range interactions between atoms and levitated nanospheres, and to utilize these platforms for highly sensitive impulsive force sensing.
main_result: The authors successfully observed single momentum kicks from Xe atom collisions, confirming the ability to measure impulsive forces down to levels significantly below the zero-point fluctuations of the oscillator.
method: The experiment uses matched filtering on time-traces of the levitated nanosphere's motion to extract discrete momentum kicks caused by collisions with a supersonic beam of Xe atoms.
model_or_system: The physical system involves a silica nanosphere levitated in an optical tweezer and cooled to its quantum ground state. Collisions are induced by a pulsed, directional beam of Xe atoms generated via supersonic expansion.
key_observables: Momentum transfer ($\Delta p$), event rate (counts/s), and the time-of-flight ($t_{	ext{TOF}}$) of the atomic beam.
important_parameters: The minimum resolvable momentum (SQL) is calculated to be $11.8$ keV/c for the given parameters. The measured sensitivity confirms detection below $50$ keV/c.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the residual signal amplitude outside the primary detection window remains below the noise threshold, and it notes limitations regarding quantitative comparison with theory due to beam size effects.
figures_summary: Figures show the setup schematic, the measured phonon occupation number, and time-traces/histograms comparing the event rate from the supersonic Xe beam against the background rate from thermal atoms.
paper_structure: The paper details the setup (trapping, cooling, beam generation), the methodology (matched filtering, rate analysis), and presents results confirming the detection of directional momentum kicks from the atomic beam.
why_interesting: This work directly bridges quantum optics (levitation, ground state cooling) with atomic physics (supersonic beams) to create an ultra-sensitive quantum sensor, which is highly relevant for open quantum systems and quantum measurement theory.

Its motion is detected via interferometric readout, in which backscattered light is combined with a local oscillator and measured with a balanced photodetector (BPD). A supersonic beam of Xe atoms is produced by a pulsed valve in the expansion chamber (bottom right). The atomic beam is subsequently collimated by a skimmer and directed toward the levitated particle through a connecting tube between the two chambers.
